{"id": "18:8/q05", "question": "What does juruz mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether juruz simply describes barrenness, specifically prior growth stripped away, inherent failure to grow, the ground's shape, ruin, cutting, confinement, or a place name.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q05/p1", "position": "Barren, bare land with no vegetation or growth.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's barren plain is transmitted repeatedly; Qatāda describes no trees, plants or buildings; Ibn Zayd says nothing useful remains. Al-Majāz cites Dhū al-Rumma for infertile land and dry years; al-Ṭabarī cites rajaz on ajrāz years; al-Māwardī cites rajaz on years stripping land. Al-Zajjāj gives the plural ajrāz. Abū ʿUbayda, transmitted by Ibn al-Jawzī, calls the ground coarse and the year drought-struck. Al-Ālūsī treats Qatāda's no-vegetation sense as apparent. Al-Bāqir's report through al-Qummī agrees."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p2", "position": "Land stripped of vegetation after it grew, by cutting, grazing, drought, locusts, or consumption.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ describes animals and locusts eating growth; Abū Muslim derives the root from cutting, like a sharp sword or all-consuming eater. Al-Kisāʾī describes people consuming every crop. Al-Bayḍāwī traces it to cutting. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says jarazat is loss through drought or locusts and corrects al-Zajjāj: the land has not grown, rather than being unable to grow. Al-Zajjāj likens the land to something that devours plants, and Ibn al-Anbārī says it consumes or burns every plant. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn cite gluttonous-woman usage, with poetic or comic lines; al-Rāzī adds the destructive sword."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p3", "position": "Land that does not grow anything.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj states this, including the picture of land consuming plants; Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly corrects this wording to land that has not grown."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p4", "position": "Smooth or level ground.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Muqātil's gloss; other descriptions of the resulting plain also stress its smoothness."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p5", "position": "Ruined or desolate land.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr are reported with the ruin gloss. Al-Ālūsī reports it through Ibn Abī Ḥātim but disputes its status as the genuine lexical sense."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p6", "position": "Cut down or harvested.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this further explanation of the transformed earth."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p7", "position": "Enclosed or confined.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī attributes this gloss to Ibn Baḥr."}, {"id": "18:8/q05/p8", "position": "Al-Jurz is a land's proper name.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī records the name in al-Itqān."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q06", "question": "How is jarz pronounced in different dialects?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q06/p1", "position": "Its vowel patterns vary among the dialects of Hijaz, Asad and Tamim.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī transmits al-Farrāʾ's account of the dialectal vowel patterns, without a preference in this note."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q07", "question": "What does the promised change do to the earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the image describes a physical barren earth, the severance of attachment, or the manifestation of divine reality and annihilation.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q07/p1", "position": "God removes the earth's adornment and life, leaving an actual level, dry, barren surface.", "reasons": "Muqātil says mountains and plants disappear as at first creation; al-Thaʿlabī says it cannot grow anything; al-Zamakhsharī pictures the green earth turning white. Al-Biqāʿī describes greenery stripped and exposed to sun and wind. Ibn Kathīr says no growth or benefit remains. Al-Ālūsī contrasts the bare soil with the scene that once delighted spectators. Abū Sahl likens it to plants cut away; al-Ṭabrisī says inhabited earth is ruined. This destruction is described as all earthly adornments or contents perishing by Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn ʿAbbās and later commentators."}, {"id": "18:8/q07/p2", "position": "The barren plain figures the ending of people's attachment to worldly adornments when the trial ends.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this metaphor: attractive goods, children and status bring souls into the earthly trial, then their attractions are removed and people stand alone for judgment. He reports the literal level-dust reading as an alternative."}, {"id": "18:8/q07/p3", "position": "The world's qualities vanish through divine manifestation and death without injustice or loss.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes true or natural death and annihilation of qualities as the way God reduces worldly adornment to the barren plain. Al-Ālūsī reports an inward account in which worldly annihilation becomes manifest when true divine existence and the greater Resurrection appear."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q08", "question": "When does the earth become barren?", "turns_on": "Whether to speak only of the final universal event or also of present local examples.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q08/p1", "position": "At the end of the world and resurrection, after earthly life and responsibility end.", "reasons": "Muqātil places it in the afterlife. The exegetes reported by Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī place the leveling at resurrection, without plants, water or shelter. Jishumī adds that moral responsibility ends, bodies perish and signs of the Hour occur. Bursawī says it is when worldly life ends; Ibn ʿĀshūr's future active participle confirms eventual ending. Kuran Yolu compares 14:48 and 55:26–27."}, {"id": "18:8/q08/p2", "position": "The process occurs in regions now and will encompass all earth at resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly distinguishes present local barrenness from its universal occurrence at resurrection; the image of drought, locusts and grazing offers present instances."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q09", "question": "What lesson does the verse draw from earthly beauty passing away?", "turns_on": "The notes draw complementary moral, consoling, evidential and grateful lessons from the same reversal.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q09/p1", "position": "People should detach from fleeting adornment and devote themselves to enduring good deeds and God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls adornment a trial before destruction and recompense. Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Kāshifī as cited by Bursawī, Elmalılı, Iṣlāḥī and Kuran Yolu warn against attachment. Bursawī urges prayer to be among those turning wholly to God; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says only deeds endure. The Study Quran reports al-Ghazālī's view that adornment tests detachment and asceticism. Elmalılı specifies service to the everlasting Creator and the best deeds, not grief over what perishes; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī at 18:42–44 says God is better in reward and outcome because He endures and people need a reliable Lord."}, {"id": "18:8/q09/p2", "position": "The Prophet should cease grieving over rejection because all worldly goods and rejecters pass away before judgment.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq, reported also by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr, says people return to God for recompense according to deeds. Abū Ḥayyān calls the verse consolation. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says people absorbed in pleasure cannot defeat God's will, citing 6:93–94; Iṣlāḥī says their blindness comes from worldly lures and they will regret it. Elmalılı counsels striving rather than wasted grief."}, {"id": "18:8/q09/p3", "position": "The reversal from flourishing to barrenness displays God's power, resurrection and the need to prepare for changing states.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says recurring restoration by rain proves resurrection and is omitted for readers of insight. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the earth is the most immediate sign to human perception, compares 88:17–20 and 51:20, and urges judging by virtue and good outcomes rather than trusting strength. Kuran Yolu cites 14:48 and 55:26–27 for the world's transformation."}, {"id": "18:8/q09/p4", "position": "The wording invites gratitude for the earth's beauty and recognition of God's artistry.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the compact wording includes these purposes, comparing 16:6 and 3:14; al-Samarrāʾī notes flowers and other delights, and the adorned sky in 15:16 and 37:6."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q10", "question": "How does this verse connect to nearby and parallel verses?", "turns_on": "How the clause completes 18:6–7 and which parallel earthly transformations illuminate it.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q10/p1", "position": "It completes the account of earth's adornment as a temporary test before its removal and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī's first coherence reading makes 18:7 explain the concern of 18:6 and 18:8 finish it; al-Rāzī cites 55:26, 20:106, 84:3 and 14:48 for destruction and transformation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clause explains the consolation of 18:6 and connects with the warning in 18:2. Asad says his bracketed interpolation supplies an implied link to the longer passage. Iṣlāḥī points forward to 18:46–48."}, {"id": "18:8/q10/p2", "position": "It consoles Muhammad after denial and warns that God will answer the rejecters.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī's second coherence reading links 18:6–7 with impending divine vengeance; the opening says the Prophet warns but cannot create faith. Ibn Isḥāq says he should not grieve over what he sees and hears; Iṣlāḥī likewise says rejection is neither a defect in the Book nor in preaching."}, {"id": "18:8/q10/p3", "position": "It urges the Prophet to continue calling rebels because God continues sustaining them, while warning against worldly attachment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this proposed link to 18:7 but calls it strained."}, {"id": "18:8/q10/p4", "position": "The barren-land image parallels 32:27, where water makes dry land produce crops.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Ibn Zayd as transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr, and al-Rāzī all cite 32:27. Their comparison shows that land can be barren and later productive."}, {"id": "18:8/q10/p5", "position": "The earth's ultimate destruction is echoed by 14:48 and 55:26–27.", "reas

{"id": "18:8/q11", "question": "Was the opening through 18:8 revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Whether reports of Medinan exceptions outweigh the reported general Meccan attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q11/p1", "position": "The whole sūra, including its opening through 18:8, is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the commentators' general view and prefers it. Ibn ʿĀshūr quotes his consensus and says proposed Medinan passages at 18:28–29 and 18:107 to the end are weak. Iṣlāḥī situates the sūra in late Makkan conflict; the Study Quran also calls it late Makkan."}, {"id": "18:8/q11/p2", "position": "The opening through the verse ending juruzan is a Medinan exception.", "reasons": "Muqātil, transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī, also excepts the believers passage at the end; al-Suyūṭī lists the patient-company command as another exception. {"id": "18:8/q12", "question": "What are the sūra's names in the reports?", "turns_on": "The reports give two names without opposing them.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q12/p1", "position": "It is called al-Kahf.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Prophet used this name; al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib's Bukhārī report names it while recounting a cloud covering a reciter beside a restless tethered horse, which the Prophet identified as tranquility descending with the Qur'an."}, {"id": "18:8/q12/p2", "position": "It is also called Sūrat Aṣḥāb al-Kahf.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Ibn Mardawayh's report attributing this name to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q13", "question": "What merits are reported for reciting al-Kahf or its opening?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in which verses, which benefit, and their assessed strength.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q13/p1", "position": "Memorizing or reciting opening verses protects from the Dajjāl.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān cites the report and interprets effective recitation as including knowledge and understanding. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Muslim and Abū Dāwūd report ten opening verses from Abū al-Dardāʾ; al-Tirmidhī reports three opening verses and grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the cited merit reports the soundest."}, {"id": "18:8/q13/p2", "position": "Memorizing ten final verses protects from the Dajjāl.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says Muslim also transmits this version and counts the previously cited merit reports as the soundest."}, {"id": "18:8/q13/p3", "position": "Friday recitation brings forgiveness through the following Friday plus three days.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this attributed merit."}, {"id": "18:8/q13/p4", "position": "Recitation brings light and protection from the grave's trial.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this as another attributed merit."}, {"id": "18:8/q13/p5", "position": "The whole sūra descended at once with seventy thousand angels.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr mentions this report among reports of varying strength and says al-Suyūṭī omitted it from al-Itqān."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q14", "question": "What is the sūra's place in revelation order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q14/p1", "position": "It followed al-Ghāshiyah, preceded al-Shūrā, and is ranked sixty-eighth by Jābir ibn Zayd.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the adjacent sūras and Jābir ibn Zayd's ordinal."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q15", "question": "How many verses does al-Kahf have in the regional counts?", "turns_on": "Regional traditions split some verses differently.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q15/p1", "position": "Medina and Mecca count 105 verses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes the differences among regional totals to different verse divisions."}, {"id": "18:8/q15/p2", "position": "Syria counts 106 verses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes the differences among regional totals to different verse divisions."}, {"id": "18:8/q15/p3", "position": "Basra counts 111 verses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes the differences among regional totals to different verse divisions."}, {"id": "18:8/q15/p4", "position": "Kufa counts 110 verses.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes the differences among regional totals to different verse divisions."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q16", "question": "What purpose and setting do commentators give the sūra?", "turns_on": "The commentators stress different narrative, historical and ethical purposes.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q16/p1", "position": "Its narratives teach rejection of association with God and piety.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the sūra presents three unusual narratives found nowhere else in the Qur'an: the Companions of the Cave, Moses and his companion, and Dhū al-Qarnayn."}, {"id": "18:8/q16/p2", "position": "It warns Quraysh in the late Makkan conflict and steadies the Prophet and believers.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Quraysh sought to erase the mission with indirect Jewish and Christian backing, risked punishment through arrogant worldly success, and the Prophet and companions were urged to patience, steadfastness, possible migration and coming victories. The Prophet's role is warning and glad tidings; unbelief is no flaw in Book or preaching."}, {"id": "18:8/q16/p3", "position": "It challenges Christians after the previous sūra exposed Jews, and warns Quraysh against following baseless opponents.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī pairs al-Kahf with Maryam in this purpose and says Quraysh risk losing God's great opportunity."}, {"id": "18:8/q16/p4", "position": "It is among the Qur'an's most excellent chapters.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives this appraisal."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q17", "question": "What does the Cave story teach in its place after this opening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q17/p1", "position": "It is an ethical parable of resurrection and faith-driven withdrawal from a wicked world.", "reasons": "Asad says the cave episode is no more wondrous than other Qur'anic messages because it fits the Qur'an's ethical teaching; whatever its origin, it depicts withdrawal rewarded by spiritual awakening beyond time and death, with 18:9–26 as context."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q18", "question": "What historical origin is proposed for the Cave story?", "turns_on": "Whether the story reflects a Christian episode, older Jewish tradition, or an Essene allegory.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q18/p1", "position": "The youths belong to early Christian history, especially persecution under Decius at Ephesus.", "reasons": "Asad says most commentators rely on the Christian legend of youths who slept for centuries; he reports the early Christian setting as their common placement."}, {"id": "18:8/q18/p2", "position": "The youths lived before Christianity.", "reasons": "Asad quotes Ibn Kathīr's reasoning that Jewish rabbis would not have preserved a Christian story after relations with Christians had broken down."}, {"id": "18:8/q18/p3", "position": "An older Jewish oral tradition underlies the later Christian telling.", "reasons": "Asad argues that the Christian version developed from pre-Christian Jewish sources."}, {"id": "18:8/q18/p4", "position": "The story's fundamentals allegorize the Essenes, especially the secluded Qumran community.", "reasons": "Asad cites the community's scriptural study, copying, preservation, seclusion and reputation for piety as likely inspiration, and notes that Jesus may have belonged to the Essenes."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q19", "question": "What does al-raqīm in the Cave story mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q19/p1", "position": "A written thing, book or scripture.", "reasons": "Asad reports Ibn ʿAbbās and early authorities equating al-raqīm with marqūm and kitāb; he reports al-Rāzī's statement that Arabic rhetoricians and philologists agree on al-kitāb."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q20", "question": "What is the cosmos beside God's power?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q20/p1", "position": "It is in God's grasp and is mere dust beside His power.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī transmits this saying of al-Wāsiṭī."}]}
{"id": "18:8/q21", "question": "How do the criminals face the Fire in the later passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb describes expectation, rushing or descent, or encounter in al-Aʿmash's reading.", "positions": [{"id": "18:8/q21/p1", "position": "The polytheists expect to enter it when they see it.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī gives the identification as polytheists. A report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet that a disbeliever sees Hell and thinks he will enter it from forty years' travel away."}, {"id": "18:8/q21/p2", "position": "They rush into or descend into it.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports these alternative glosses."}, {"id": "18:8/q21/p3", "position": "They encounter it.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī records al-Aʿmash's reading with this sense."}]}
{"id": "18:22/q01", "question": "Who are the people predicted to give these counts?", "turns_on": "Whether future speech is the Prophet's contemporaries' dispute, a retrospective report of the cave community, or continuing public discussion; reports assign denominations differently.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q01/p1", "position": "People of Scripture in the Prophet's time, variously Jews or Christian groups, voiced the counts.", "reasons": "Yahya, Ibn Hisham and Ibn Atiyya connect the Jews with questions sent through Meccans. Muqatil, Tha'labi, Wahidi and others recount Najran's Jacobite Sayyid saying three, Nestorian Aqib five, and Muslims seven; Ibn Jawzi also reports a different Melkite/Jacobite/Nestorian assignment. Alusi doubts the exclusively Jewish account."}, {"id": "18:22/q01/p2", "position": "People of the youths' own city disputed before their discovery, or people around the cave later disputed.",

{"id": "18:22/q03", "question": "How are the numbers and dog clauses parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted subject, pronoun link, participle, or explicit waw licenses each following clause.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q03/p1", "position": "Each number is a nominative predicate of omitted 'they'; the dog clause describes the number or serves as another predicate.", "reasons": "Farra and Zajjaj reject accusative object syntax. Nahhas supplies subjects. Zamakhshari, Nasafi and Samin make dog clauses adjectival; Ibn Ashur also permits successive predicates. Abu Hayyan and Samin supply 'persons', not 'men', because the dog makes the total four. Razi notes omitted 'they'; Burhan compares 3:13. Alusi reports Ibn al-Hajib's successive-predicate analysis. Tabatabai transmits Zamakhshari's parse."}, {"id": "18:22/q03/p2", "position": "The dog clause is a circumstantial clause attached to the count.", "reasons": "Tha'lab calls the last waw circumstantial; Sahib al-Nazm takes the first clause as a circumstance of three. Abu al-Fath objects that 'they are three' offers no governor. Ibn Ashur makes the last clause circumstantial."}, {"id": "18:22/q03/p3", "position": "'Fourth' adjectivally modifies 'three' and governs 'their dog' as an active participle.", "reasons": "One grammatical proposal uses participial government. Abu al-Fath and Abu al-Baqa object that a past participle cannot work this way; Samin answers that the past scene is depicted as present, like basit."}, {"id": "18:22/q03/p4", "position": "The dog clause describes the group as an independent subject-predicate sentence.", "reasons": "The example 'these are three, their servant fourth' supports it; Abu al-Fath objects that the final conjunction requires parallel coordination, with earlier conjunctions omitted through pronominal linkage."}, {"id": "18:22/q03/p5", "position": "The dog clauses are coordinated sentences whose conjunction can be understood where absent.", "reasons": "Abu al-Fath and Abu Ali say pronominal reference links earlier clauses without an overt conjunction; Wahidi makes 'fourth' coordinate with the initial predicate. Tabrisi says shared reference permits either overt or omitted conjunction, but denies treating the last clause as a mere description."}]}
{"id": "18:22/q04", "question": "How is the three-count pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q04/p1", "position": "Ibn Muhaysin assimilates the final thāʾ of 'three' to the following tāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite proximity of articulation, common voicelessness, and the preceding alif or weak letter; Kashshaf and Ibn Atiyya report it too."}]}
{"id": "18:22/q05", "question": "How is the five-count pronounced?", "turns_on": "Transmitted vowel and assimilation variants and the strength of their attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q05/p1", "position": "A report from Ibn Kathir opens the mīm of khamsa with fatḥa.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi call it transmitted dialectal usage and compare ʿashara; Ibn Jinni says poetic necessity is not required and compares variant place-name forms."}, {"id": "18:22/q05/p2", "position": "Ibn Muhaysin is reported with kasra on khāʾ and mīm and assimilation into the following sīn.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi add a variant assimilating tanwīn without nasalization. Samin calls the reading very heavy and suspects mistaken attribution. Ibn Atiyya reports vowel variation."}]}
{"id": "18:22/q06", "question": "How many youths were in the cave?", "turns_on": "Whether the uncriticized final count and waw establish seven, whether 'dog' conceals an eighth man, and whether the divine reservation counsels withholding a precise answer.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q06/p1", "position": "Seven youths, with the dog eighth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas repeatedly counts himself among the few and says seven; Abu Masud and others concur. Tha'labi, Kashshaf, Baydawi and Nasafi say Muslims learned this from the Prophet through Gabriel. Many argue that only three and five are labeled conjecture; Razi adds the emphatic waw, the following 'few know', likelihood that one reported count is true, and revelation to the Prophet. Ibn Kathir calls Ibn Abbas chains sound. Ali's reported seven include six royal advisers and a shepherd; transmitted name spellings vary. Alusi questions the Ali attribution and the inference that few early hearers perceived the linguistic clue. Tabatabai adds the earlier dialogue's implication of at least seven."}, {"id": "18:22/q06/p2", "position": "Eight youths, with the eighth understood as the dog's owner or companion.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Ishaq construe 'eighth' with an implied owner or companion; the noncanonical kalbihim or kalbihim reading is taken as 'their herder' or dog's owner. Ibn Kathir cautions that an eight-name report from Mujahid may come from Ibn Ishaq or an intermediary; Bagawi calls seven correct."}, {"id": "18:22/q06/p3", "position": "Three youths, with the dog fourth.", "reasons": "Najran Jacobite or Melkite speakers, or Jews in another report, make this first claim. The Quran labels it conjecture. A discrepant Suddi report has Ibn Abbas tentatively guess three despite many reports of his seven."}, {"id": "18:22/q06/p4", "position": "Five youths, with the dog sixth.", "reasons": "Reports variously assign it to Najran Nestorians or Jacobites, or Christians generally; it is explicitly called conjecture."}, {"id": "18:22/q06/p5", "position": "The revealed wording leaves the exact count with God rather than establishing a count for readers.", "reasons": "Islahi calls the seven inference plausible but prefers the verse's reserve. {"id": "18:22/q07", "question": "What do reports say about the youths' identities and setting?", "turns_on": "The value and reliability of transmitted names and geographical traditions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q07/p1", "position": "Lists name seven youths, often six royal advisers and a seventh shepherd, in or near Ephesus.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Ibn Abbas, Ali and Hushaym give names with unstable foreign spellings; some call Yamlikha the food purchaser. {"id": "18:22/q10", "question": "What does 'rajman bil-ghayb' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase's scope includes both preceding claims and whether the unqualified seven count is thereby endorsed.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q10/p1", "position": "It means guessing or speaking conjecturally about an unseen matter without knowledge.", "reasons": "Qatada and Suddi gloss it thus. {"id": "18:22/q14", "question": "What does 'my Lord knows best their number' assert?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's reservation simply states divine epistemic priority or also withholds any definitive human count.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q14/p1", "position": "God has complete and certain knowledge of the count; humans know only what He discloses.", "reasons": "Damghani glosses idda as number or count. {"id": "18:22/q21", "question": "What wider rule about knowledge or legal opinion is drawn from the prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's rebuke of unsupported claims applies generally to transmitted knowledge or conjectural legal reasoning.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q21/p1", "position": "Some infer Muslims should not seek religious rulings or knowledge from Jews and Christians.", "reasons": "Wahidi's associates infer a prohibition on religious rulings; Jishumi says reports of unbelievers are unreliable; Qurtubi sees the Najran story as proof against consultation on knowledge."}, {"id": "18:22/q21/p2", "position": "Opponents of analogical legal reasoning cite condemnation of guessing as forbidding conjectural fatwas.", "reasons": "Razi reports their use of 'rajman bil-ghayb' and a Kashshaf poetry line where rajm means mere supposition; he presents it as their argument, not his own verdict."}]}
{"id": "18:22/q22", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from the youths and their dog?", "turns_on": "Which elements of the surface story serve as symbols: cognitive faculties, saints, companionship, or divine knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "18:22/q22/p1", "position": "The seven youths represent faculties of cognition and action; the dog represents the lower self.", "reasons": "Qashani maps seven to two intellects, thought, estimation, imagination, memory and common sense; a related royal-adviser report maps the king to the commanding self, right advisers to intellect and thought, left advisers to imagination, estimation and memory, and shepherd to common sense.
